US stocks edged lower Thursday, snapping a rebound that had lifted the S&P 500 1.3% a day earlier. The S&P 500 fell 0.35% to 7,592.40, the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.36% to 52,297.09, and the Nasdaq Composite lost 0.39% to 25,366.09, Yahoo Finance reported, as bond yields rose. Traders weighed hot inflation data, the Federal Reserve's next move and higher oil prices.

Buy Alert: 10 Stocks Analysts Upgraded on Wednesday

Photo by Pascal Bernardon on Unsplash

Hot Inflation Keeps the Fed in Focus

The week's moves have been shaped by interest rates. Tuesday's hotter-than-expected inflation report convinced traders that the Federal Reserve will raise rates next month, Reuters said. According to CME FedWatch, investors fully price in a hike of at least 25 basis points, with a 13.2% chance of a 50-basis-point move. Several Fed officials have said they are open to a more aggressive path, and Wall Street analysts have raised their forecasts for more and bigger hikes, Yahoo Finance said.

Wednesday's rebound showed how quickly sentiment can swing. The S&P 500 gained 1.3% and the Nasdaq Composite 1.6% after results from an AI cloud company eased worries about the durability of the artificial intelligence trade, Reutersreported, with advancing stocks outnumbering decliners by 1.3 to 1 on the NYSE. The Treasury market was closed for Veterans Day, so bond traders could react only on Thursday.

Oil Adds to the Uncertainty

Thursday brought another pressure point. Oil prices climbed after the president said he was no longer interested in a deal with Iran, the Associated Press reported, which complicates the inflation outlook. Higher energy costs feed into the same inflation numbers the Fed is fighting. Even so, the S&P 500 finished with a modest loss and is up 2.9% for the week.

Retail investors are watching the same swings closely, and Reddit threads tend to cluster around names where the gap between price and analyst expectations looks widest. That gap deserves some care. An average price target is a twelve-month estimate pulled from sell-side analysts, it is often revised after earnings, and a handful of outliers can skew the mean. Because upside is measured against the current share price, a sharp drop widens it overnight, while a rally shrinks it just as fast. title: Warren Buffett's Berkshire Compounded at More Than 19% a Year Over Six Decades, Nearly Double the S&P 500's 10% Return. Can Investors Still Apply That Playbook Today?
detail:
Warren Buffett's Berkshire Compounded at More Than 19% a Year Over Six Decades, Nearly Double the S&P 500's 10% Return. Can Investors Still Apply That Playbook Today?
Prosper Junior Bakiny, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 9:54 AM PST 5 min read
BRK-B
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Warren Buffett is widely considered to be the greatest investor of all time. That's not an official title, but there is tangible data supporting the Oracle of Omaha's stellar reputation. As the head of Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRKA) (NYSE:BRKB), Buffett delivered average annual returns of more than 19% over six decades. It's hard enough to beat the market over a single 10-year period. Doing it for 60 years is extraordinary. But can investors still apply Buffett's principles in today's market? Let's find out.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The Warren Buffett way

Buffett's investing strategy sounds simple on the surface. It boils down to buying shares in companies with strong moats at attractive prices and holding onto them for a long time. However, there is a lot more hiding under the hood. And we can glean important lessons from certain details.

For instance, Warren Buffett has historically avoided certain sectors, including technology. That doesn't mean Berkshire Hathaway has never invested in any tech company. But Buffett himself focuses primarily on relatively simple businesses he understands well, that generate steady cash flows, and have business models that remain more or less unchanged over the long run.

This is an important aspect of the Oracle of Omaha's investing philosophy. The easier it is to forecast a company's future cash flows, the easier it tends to be to determine when it is trading at an attractive price, since, according to one school of investing, a business' intrinsic value is just the value of all of its future cash flows discounted at an appropriate rate.

Buffett's long-term mindset is another important aspect of his strategy. It's always difficult to predict a stock's short-term movement, but as Benjamin Graham, Buffett's mentor, once said: "In the short run, the stock market is a voting machine. But in the long run, it is a weighing machine." Since value drives long-term performance, short-term volatility is no reason to panic-sell.

Staying put over the long run also grants investors tax advantages while putting the magic of compounding to good use, especially with dividend stocks. This isn't quite all there is to Buffett's strategy. But it's a good start.

Here's how to do it

Emulating Buffett isn't easy. Investors certainly shouldn't expect returns similar to those of the Oracle of Omaha. If it were easy to pull that off, any number of Wall Street hedge fund managers would, but in fact, many of them fail to do so. Warren Buffett once bet $1 million that a low-cost index fund would outperform a group of hedge funds over a decade.

title: The S&P 500 Has Gone 18 Months Without a 10% Drop. Here's How the Next Year Has Gone After Streaks This Long.
detail:
The S&P 500 Has Gone 18 Months Without a 10% Drop. Here's How the Next Year Has Gone After Streaks This Long.
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 8:58 AM PST 5 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) last closed in correction territory on April 28, 2025. It ended the day at 5,528.75, just over 10% under the record close of 6,144.15 it had set on Feb. 19.

Since then, every close has stayed within 10% of a record. In other words, the index has gone more than 380 trading days, or about 18 months, without what investors normally call a correction (a fall of 10% or more from a peak).

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Even the 4.36% drop on Nov. 5, when chipmakers and other companies linked to artificial intelligence sold off, left the index only about 6% under its high close of 7,818.93 on Oct. 6.

As I write, the S&P 500 is near 7,520, about 4% under that record. It would take a close below about 7,037 to snap the streak.

A run like this can make an index fund investor wonder if a fall is coming. I looked back through the index's history for every past stretch since 1950 that lasted this long, and found seven. A year after each one reached this length, the index was higher in five of them, with a median gain of around 7%.

That isn't far from how an ordinary year has gone, and I don't think it looks like a warning sign.

Image source: Getty Images.

Only seven stretches have lasted this long

I counted a streak as every session in a row that finished less than 10% under the index's record close through that day, with Yahoo Finance's daily closes (which don't include dividends). Then I measured each past streak from the session when it matched the current run's length.

The early 1950s saw none, because the index remained more than 10% below its 1929 high until May 1954.

Two of the seven reached this length in the 1960s, another two in 1986 and 1992, and the last three in 2014, 2017, and 2022. The shortest began in mid-2020 and ended in February 2022. The longest started in early 1991 and lasted until October 1997, nearly seven years later.

Five of the seven were higher a year later

A year after reaching this length, the S&P 500 was up in five of the seven cases. The largest gain followed the 1986 mark, at around 28%. The smallest followed 1992, at about 6%.

For all seven, the median and the average were both gains of around 7%.

The smaller of the two losses followed January 1960. In the next 12 months, the index dipped by around 2%, a period that included a recession that began that April, according to National Bureau of Economic Research dates.

Most investors know that artificial intelligence stocks are responsible for the bulk of the broad market's gains since the 2022 bear market. What's not quite as obvious is that most of this strong performance was led by large-cap stocks. The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC), a market cap-weighted index, is up about 110% since the current bull market began.

For perspective, the S&P 600 Small Cap Index has only gained 72% over the same period. Growth stocks have also outpaced value stocks during this stretch.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

As the old adage goes, though, nothing lasts forever. The cyclical underpinnings of this disparate performance may be on the verge of reversing, working against large-cap stocks -- and AI mega caps in particular -- and in favor of small-cap stocks. Specifically, they're working in favor of small-cap value stocks.

This changing dynamic bodes well for a holding like the Vanguard Morningstar Small-Cap Value ETF (NYSEMKT: VBR), which could end up outperforming the S&P 500 and its exchange-traded funds (ETFs), like the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEMKT: SPY), over the coming decade.

It's already happening, in fact.

Time for a change

It's gone largely unnoticed due to the inordinate amount of noise of late. But small-cap value stocks have handily beaten the S&P 500's year-to-date gain of just over 12%, with nearly a 20% gain of their own.

^CVK data by YCharts.

Granted, much of this gap is the result of several AI stocks recently running into a wall of fiscal reality. It's also a shift that's been brewing quietly for a while, waiting for the right time to take hold.

That time may be now. As asset management outfit AllianceBernstein's analysts highlighted earlier this year (based on numbers from FactSet), "[T]he Russell 2000 earnings growth is now expected to outpace S&P 500 profits through the second half of 2026 and 2027." The analysis adds, for good measure: "[T]he sector profile of small-caps transcends AI themes." At the same time, data from Yardeni Research indicates that the S&P 600's forward-looking price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio currently stands at just over 14, which is actually below its long-term average. It could take a decade to renormalize these valuations.

Conversely, the S&P 500's cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio currently stands near a multi-decade high around 40, last seen in early 2000. Although its more familiar trailing P/E ratio of 22 and forward-looking P/E ratio of 19 are both lower, both are also still somewhat above their long-term norms.

A $1 million all-stock retiree who started the 4% rule in January 2000 had about $96,000 left at the end of 2025; a neighbor who started in January 2003 had $6.1 million. The same fund, the same rule, three years apart.

The S&P 500 lost 37.6% from 2000 through 2002 while the first retiree withdrew $123,870; by January 2003 her withdrawal was 8.0% of what was left, and by January 2009 it was 13.1%.

Bengen's rule assumed 50% to 75% in stocks with the rest in Treasuries. With half her money in 10-year Treasuries the first retiree would have ended 2025 with $1,279,287; skipping the inflation raise after each losing year, all in stocks, would have left her $780,840.

The biggest 401k decisions tend to get made once and never revisited: when to roll it over, what to hold inside it, and when to start taking money out. That is exactly what the report: 401k & IRA Tips and Answers was created to address, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

A woman who retired at 64 in January 2000 with $1 million in an S&P 500 index fund, took $40,000 out that first year and gave herself an inflation raise every January after that had about $96,000 left at the end of 2025. Her neighbor, who retired at 64 in January 2003 with the same $1 million, the same fund and the same 4% rule, had $6.1 million.

Both retirees are scenarios, and the gap between them is real. Each year's result comes from the S&P 500's published total return for that calendar year (price change plus dividends) and the Bureau of Labor Statistics' annual inflation rate, which sets each January's raise. There are no fees, taxes or Social Security in the math; both women would have had a Social Security check, and it is left out because it would be the same for each of them.

The gap is sequence of returns risk: the fund earned about 8.1% a year over the 26 years, but the first retiree sold shares into three straight losing years before any of the good ones arrived, and a withdrawal plan never gets back what it sells at the bottom. The limit on that reading is that she broke William Bengen's rule before the market did. The 4% rule was built on a portfolio with half its money in bonds, and with half of hers in 10-year Treasuries she would have ended 2025 with about $1.3 million, more than she started with.

title: Should You Invest in the Stock Market Now or Wait for a Pullback? History Offers a Clear Answer.
detail:
Should You Invest in the Stock Market Now or Wait for a Pullback? History Offers a Clear Answer.
David Dierking, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 6:56 AM PST 5 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

After a volatile post-election market, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) now sits about 4% below its all-time high, but the Nasdaq-100 is down by roughly 11%. Anybody waiting to buy the dip certainly has an opportunity right now. But whether they take it is something else altogether.

Down markets tend to bring out some of the worst behaviors for investors. Instead of looking at scenarios like right now as chances to buy stocks on sale, they tend to view them as risky situations where stocks could fall further. Some people get so consumed with trying to find the bottom that they end up missing out on the opportunity altogether.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Investing is one of the few things where doing less is often rewarded more. But people tend to wonder about whether stocks are too expensive, or stocks could drop more, or some economic disaster is imminent. This kind of analysis paralysis can actually damage returns because they wait for something to happen that never comes.

The best path is usually just to keep doing what you're already doing.

Image source: Getty Images.
The reward for perfect timing is smaller than you think

Charles Schwab (NYSE: SCHW) published a popular study last year looking at different hypothetical investors who invested their money in different ways. Each invested $2,000 annually over the course of 20 years:

"Peter Perfect" invested his money at the lowest point every year.

"Ashley Action" invested her money on the first trading day of the year.

"Matthew Monthly" invested his money in 12 equal portions at the beginning of each month.

"Rosie Rotten" invested her money at the highest point every year.

"Larry Linger" left his money in cash and never invested in stocks at all.

The results were surprisingly close given the different approaches. Peter, not surprisingly, did best with an ending balance of $186,077. But Ashley and Matthew weren't that far behind with $170,555 and $166,591, respectively. Even $151,343 accumulated by Rosie was a substantial gain on her investment. Larry, with all of his money in cash, finished with just $47,357 and proved a very important point.

The biggest factor for building long-term wealth is simply being invested in stocks. The gap between being a flawless market timer and just investing on a regular set schedule is pretty modest. Being right pays off little, but being wrong costs a lot.

There's been no shortage of market volatility over the last week. After experiencing their worst week of 2026 in early November, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC), and Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) are rallying once again.

However, that doesn't mean that investors are in the clear. The tech industry is still struggling with volatility -- especially after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's recent ousting -- and the market is the priciest it's been in decades.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Warren Buffett has also issued a direct warning to investors who may be underestimating market risk right now, and history has both good and bad news about what's coming next.

Warren Buffett. Image source: The Motley Fool.

Buffett warns that some investors are "gambling"

During Berkshire Hathaway's 2026 meeting, Buffett discussed his thoughts on the current market in an interview with CNBC. He warned that in this historically expensive market, some investors are taking on too much risk.

"I've compared the markets to a church with a casino attached," he noted, with the church representing fundamentals-based long-term investing and the casino depicting short-term buying.

[T]he casino has gotten very attractive to people," Buffett warned, adding, "that's not investing, it's not speculating, it's gambling." He emphasized, however, that "that doesn't mean that investing is terrible. It does mean that prices for an awful lot of things will look very silly."

What history says is coming next

The S&P 500 has notched more than two dozen record highs so far in 2026, but the downside to all of that growth is that some stocks are at risk of becoming overvalued.

The S&P 500 Shiller CAPE Ratio measures the S&P 500's valuation over time based on its 10-year inflation-adjusted earnings. The higher the metric climbs, the more likely the index is overvalued and due for a pullback.

Shiller CAPE Ratio data by YCharts

While no market indicator can predict when recessions or bear markets will begin, this particular metric has a long track record of preceding downturns. In 1929, for example, it spiked just before the Great Depression began. It surged again in 1999, during the dot-com bubble. Most recently, it peaked in late 2021, just months before stocks sank into a bear market.
